title: Hoffman v. Blaski (1960)
summary: The defendant could not make an otherwise ineligible transferee forum eligible simply by consenting to suit there after the action began.
notes:
The casebook notes the later statutory addition permitting transfer to a district to which all parties consent. Preserve the historical holding while reading that later language; the decision is not a prohibition on the all-party-consent route.

Illinois plaintiffs sued a Texas corporation for patent infringement in Texas; the Texas district court transferred the case to Illinois, and the Seventh Circuit issued mandamus because the defendant could not have been served in Illinois and the action could not have been brought there. The Court held 1404(a) permits transfer only to a district where the plaintiff had a right to bring the action, regardless of defendant consent.

Justice Whittaker wrote the majority; Justice Frankfurter dissented, joined by Justices Harlan and Brennan.

sections.Parties: The litigation involved defendants seeking transfer of actions, including a patent action, to districts the plaintiffs could not originally have selected under the governing requirements.
sections.Material Facts: The defendants preferred a different federal district and were willing to waive objections to litigating there. At the time of filing, however, the plaintiff did not have the independent ability to bring the action in that district. The transfer proposal thus depended on the defendant’s later consent rather than on the statutory characteristics of the proposed forum at the action’s commencement.
sections.Procedural History: The Supreme Court considered the validity of transfers under § 1404(a) and rejected the defendants’ construction of the transferee-eligibility language.
sections.Issue: Did a defendant’s consent make the proposed destination a district where the action “might have been brought” under the statute as then written?
sections.Holding: No. Eligibility under that language depended on where the plaintiff had a right to bring the action independently of the defendant’s later wishes.
sections.Reasoning: The threshold language limited which destinations a court could consider before weighing convenience and the interests of justice. Allowing defendants alone to confer eligibility by a post-filing waiver would give the statute a meaning dependent on their preferences and would weaken that threshold. The convenience analysis therefore could not begin by assuming that any district acceptable to the moving defendant was authorized. The opinion distinguishes consent capable of waiving personal objections from the separate interpretation of Congress’s transfer authorization.

learning.why: The defendant could not make an otherwise ineligible transferee forum eligible simply by consenting to suit there after the action began.

topics.cp-transfer: The transferee district had to qualify under the statute’s where-it-might-have-been-brought language. A defendant’s unilateral willingness to litigate elsewhere did not create original eligibility under the version applied.
topics.cp-procedure-merits: Convenience did not dispense with the transfer statute’s threshold requirements.
topics.cp-judicial-discretion: Hoffman places a statutory limit on transfer discretion: the transferee court must satisfy the statutory authorization discussed in the opinion.
topics.cp-usc-1404: The case construes the 'where it might have been brought' language of 1404(a) itself.
topics.cp-venue: Transfer eligibility turned on whether venue and service were proper in the transferee district at filing, independent of defendant consent.

learning.separateOpinions: The dissent favored a more flexible reading that would permit transfer to a convenient forum where the defendant consented and could defend.

mnemonic.rationale: A transfer to a district that could not have heard the case
